summary: Describes TAMP, a transport-independent protocol for managing trust anchors and community identifiers in a trust anchor store. It uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax and digital signatures for integrity and origin authentication. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
A trust anchor is a public key that the device trusts to decide which signatures are genuine. TAMP is the protocol that lets a manager install, replace and check those keys on a device.

Every request is signed, so the device knows who sent it, and carries a counter so that an old request cannot be replayed.

questions: what is an apex trust anchor
how do you manage trust anchors
subtitle: A protocol for installing, replacing and checking the public keys a device trusts.

tldr.problem: A device that checks digital signatures needs a set of trusted public keys, and those keys have to be installed, replaced and audited without the device being physically handled.
tldr.mechanism: TAMP defines eleven signed or unsigned messages, carried in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, that a trust anchor manager sends to a trust anchor store to add, change or remove trust anchors, to query what is installed, and to manage community identifiers.
tldr.outcome: A device can be told to trust a new key, to drop an old one, or to report what it trusts, with replay protection from a per-signer sequence number and authorisation checked by subordination rules. The document is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Messages before the counter runs out

today: RFC 5934 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the protocol itself; the trust anchor format it uses comes from RFC 5914 and the certificates from RFC 5280. The document also describes an HTTP binding in Appendix C, so the messages can be carried over a web request.

sections.title: What TAMP Is For
sections.content:
This document describes the Trust Anchor Management Protocol, TAMP. TAMP may be used to manage the trust anchors and community identifiers in any device that uses digital signatures, although the specification was written with the requirements of cryptographic modules in mind. One example is signed firmware packages, where the trust anchor public key can validate the digital signatures on a firmware package, or validate the X.509 certification path of the package signer.

Most TAMP messages are digitally signed, which gives integrity protection and data origin authentication. Both signed and unsigned TAMP messages use the Cryptographic Message Syntax, the container used for signed email, and that container is built on ASN.1.

The specification does not provide for confidentiality. If confidentiality is needed, the environment that carries the messages has to provide it. The document is intended to satisfy the protocol requirements expressed in the Trust Anchor Management Requirements specification.

TAMP messages may be exchanged in real time over a network, for example over HTTP, or they may be stored and transferred by other means. An exchange consists of a request message that carries instructions for a trust anchor store and, optionally, a response message that reports the result. Responses need not always come back: a GPS receiver may be unable to transmit one and may instead show the result on a display.
sections.plainLanguage: A trust anchor is a public key that the device trusts to decide which signatures are genuine. TAMP is the protocol that lets a manager install, replace and check those keys on a device.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Trust Anchor
sections.content:
A trust anchor contains a public key used to validate digital signatures. TAMP recognises three formats for representing that information: a certificate, a TBSCertificate, and the TrustAnchorInfo structure of RFC 5914. All trust anchors are distinguished by their public key, and all of them consist of a public key signature algorithm identifier with its public key, which may include parameters, and a public key identifier. Other information may appear too, such as certification path processing controls and a human-readable name.

The public key names a trust anchor, and the public key identifier says which trust anchor signed a particular object, such as a SignedData object or a certificate. The identifier can be stored with the trust anchor, or, with most assignment methods, computed from the public key when it is needed.

A trust anchor public key can be used in two ways. In the first, it validates the digital signature directly. In the second, it validates an X.509 certification path, and the subject public key in the final certificate of that path validates the signature. With the second approach the certified public key may be used for other things too, and what it may be used for is limited by the key usage certificate extension. TAMP implementations MUST support messages validated directly with a trust anchor; support for messages validated through a certificate or a longer path is OPTIONAL.

TAMP recognises three types of trust anchor by function. Identity trust anchors are used to validate certification paths and represent the trust anchor of a public key infrastructure; they are most often used for certificates in non-management applications. Management trust anchors are used in the management of cryptographic modules: the TAMP messages themselves are validated to a management trust anchor, and so is a signed firmware package. Apex trust anchors are the authority over a trust anchor store, and the apex trust anchor private key is expected to be held by an entity with information assurance responsibility for the store.

Within one trust anchor store, one trust anchor is superior to all others. That is the apex trust anchor, and it represents the ultimate authority over the store. Much of that authority can be delegated to other trust anchors. Because of its special nature, TAMP has separate facilities for changing it, including a way to replace it securely. That action might be taken because the crypto period of the key pair has ended, because the private key is no longer available, because the key pair has to be revoked, because the authority has decided on a different signature algorithm or key size, or because it has decided to transfer control to another authority.

To allow this, the apex trust anchor MAY include two public keys. Whenever the apex trust anchor is updated, both are replaced. The first, the operational public key, is used like any other trust anchor, and any TAMP message, including an Apex Trust Anchor Update, can be validated with it. The second, the contingency public key, can only be used to update the apex trust anchor. Its private key SHOULD be used at only one point in time, to sign an Apex Trust Anchor Update message that replaces it and the operational public key. The contingency public key is distributed in encrypted form, and the symmetric key needed to decrypt it travels inside the signed Apex Trust Anchor Update message that it is used to verify.

Apex trust anchors and management trust anchors that sign TAMP messages also have a sequence number, used for replay detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of trust anchor do three jobs: the apex one runs the store, a management one controls updates, and an identity one is the root of a certificate system. The apex one can also carry a spare key that is only ever used to replace the apex key itself.

sections.title: The Parts of a TAMP System
sections.content:
TAMP does not assume any particular architecture, but it requires four elements. A cryptographic module holds the private key used to sign responses, and it must support at least one one-way hash function, one digital signature validation algorithm, one digital signature generation algorithm and, if contingency keys are supported, one symmetric key unwrapping algorithm. The document does not mandate any particular algorithm.

A trust anchor store keeps the trust anchors. It must have a unique name, it should be able to store one or more community identifiers, and if it supports an apex trust anchor it must store exactly one. Each trust anchor must have a unique public key, and a public key MUST NOT appear twice in the same store. The store must also hold a sequence number for each trust anchor that is allowed to sign TAMP messages, and be able to report it together with the key identifier.

TAMP processing is the part that handles the protocol itself. It must be able to find a suitable trust anchor, either by public key identifier or by the trust anchor's distinguished name and certification path controls; the first method MUST be supported and the second MAY be. It must be able to invoke the signature validation algorithm with the public key held in secure storage, and it must have read and write access to the sequence numbers, to the trust anchors themselves and to the community membership list.

Application-specific protocol processing is the rest of the device's use of trust anchors. Applications MUST make sure that the use of a trust anchor is consistent with the constraints attached to it. For example, if name constraints are attached to a trust anchor, certification paths that start at that trust anchor and contain certificates with names that break the constraints MUST be rejected. Non-management applications SHOULD only use identity trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: Four parts have to be there: the module that holds the signing key, the store that holds the trust anchors, the code that runs the protocol, and the rest of the device that uses the trust anchors for its own work.

sections.title: How a TAMP Message Is Wrapped
sections.content:
TAMP uses signed and unsigned messages, and both are built with the Cryptographic Message Syntax. A digital signature protects a message from undetected modification and identifies who sent it. TAMP makes no general provision for encrypting content.

For a signed message, the outermost layer is always the CMS ContentInfo structure, which wraps the CMS SignedData content type, and SignedData in turn wraps the TAMP message. The version number is always 3, there is exactly one digest algorithm and exactly one signer. The signed attributes are required in TAMP messages, and the unsigned attributes may only be present in an Apex Trust Anchor Update message. A unique content type identifier says which kind of TAMP message it is.

For an unsigned message, the outermost layer is still ContentInfo, but it wraps the TAMP message directly, and the content type identifier names the message type.

When a TAMP message replaces the apex trust anchor, the same structure is used, but the signature is validated with either the operational public key or the contingency public key. When the contingency key is used, the symmetric key needed to decrypt the stored contingency public key travels as an unsigned attribute of the message being verified.

The encoding of all of this is ASN.1, the notation used to describe data protocols, with the Basic Encoding Rules or their Distinguished Encoding Rules subset. The Basic Encoding Rules offer more than one way to represent a data structure, which is not desirable when digital signatures are involved, so the Distinguished Encoding Rules were invented to give exactly one way to represent a given value. Digitally signed structures MUST be encoded with them, and in this specification the Distinguished Encoding Rules are REQUIRED for all structures, which leaves the processor fewer choices to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Every TAMP message is wrapped in the same container that signed email uses. A signed message has the signature inside that container. All of it is encoded in a way that gives exactly one possible representation for each value, so that a signature covers one unambiguous string.

sections.title: The Eleven Message Types
sections.content:
TAMP specifies eleven message types, and each has its own object identifier, used as the content type in the container. Some messages MUST be signed, and an implementation MUST reject a message of that type that is not signed. The others SHOULD be signed.

  • The TAMP Status Query message, identifier 1, MUST be signed. It asks what trust anchors are installed in a store and which communities the store belongs to.
  • The TAMP Status Response message, identifier 2, SHOULD be signed. It answers that question, in a terse or a verbose form, and the store MUST support both.
  • The Trust Anchor Update message, identifier 3, MUST be signed. It adds, modifies or removes trust anchors.
  • The Trust Anchor Update Confirm message, identifier 4, SHOULD be signed.
  • The Apex Trust Anchor Update message, identifier 5, MUST be signed. It replaces the apex trust anchor.
  • The Apex Trust Anchor Update Confirm message, identifier 6, SHOULD be signed.
  • The Community Update message, identifier 7, MUST be signed. It manages the community identifiers.
  • The Community Update Confirm message, identifier 8, SHOULD be signed.
  • The TAMP Error message, identifier 9, SHOULD be signed.
  • The Sequence Number Adjust message, identifier 10, MUST be signed.
  • The Sequence Number Adjust Confirm message, identifier 11, SHOULD be signed.

Trust anchor managers generate the Status Query, Trust Anchor Update, Apex Trust Anchor Update, Community Update and Sequence Number Adjust messages. Trust anchor stores generate the responses and the error message. Support for Trust Anchor Update is REQUIRED; support for all the other formats is RECOMMENDED. Implementations that operate in a disconnected manner MUST NOT assume a response will come back for every message they send.

A typical exchange is a status query and its response, followed by a trust anchor update and its confirmation. Each query and update message says whether it wants a terse or a verbose response, and the store SHOULD generate the kind of response that was asked for.

When an update message is processed, three checks are made. The message is authenticated, including building and validating a certification path to the signer if that is needed. The signer's authorisation is checked, including its authorisation to manage the trust anchors in the update. Then the trust anchor information to be stored is calculated. Where a trust anchor is represented as a certificate and that calculation differs from the information in the certificate, the update fails, and the signer may then wrap the certificate in a TrustAnchorInfo structure to assert the intended information.

Subordination checking is part of the validation of every Trust Anchor Update except those signed with the apex trust anchor operational public key, since the apex trust anchor is unconstrained. For an update to be valid, the signature MUST be validated using an authorised trust anchor, directly or through a certification path that starts at the apex operational public key or at an authorised management trust anchor. For each individual update in the message, the constraints of the signer MUST be greater than or equal to the constraints of the trust anchor in the update.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eleven kinds of message. Five of them are requests that a manager sends, and six are answers or errors that a store sends. Every request is signed, and a store that cannot accept an update says so with a status code.

sections.title: Replay Protection with Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
The sequence number rules are a balance between replay protection, operational realities and how much memory a store needs. The result is that sequence number checking is done on messages validated directly with a trust anchor, and may be skipped when the originator is not represented by a trust anchor. Implementations MUST check sequence numbers on messages validated directly with a trust anchor, and MAY do so for messages validated through a certification path.

The Status Query, Trust Anchor Update, Apex Trust Anchor Update, Community Update and Sequence Number Adjust messages all include a sequence number. It is a single-use identifier that matches a message with its response, and when the message is validated directly with a trust anchor the same number is used to detect replay.

For replay protection, each originator MUST treat its sequence number as a monotonically increasing non-negative integer. The counter belongs to the signing operation performed by the private key. The trust anchor store MUST ensure that a newly received message validated directly by a trust anchor public key carries a sequence number greater than the most recent successfully processed message from that originator. If it does not, the store MUST reject the message and return a sequence number failure error. The Sequence Number Adjust message is the exception: it is valid when its sequence number is greater than or equal to the most recent one.

When a trust anchor is authorised for TAMP messages, either newly installed or modified, and no sequence number is given in the update, memory is allocated for the number and set to zero. The first TAMP message validated with that trust anchor is not rejected on sequence number grounds, and its number is stored. The recipient keeps a database of the most recent sequence number from a successfully processed message from each trust anchor, indexed by the trust anchor public key.

Sequence numbers are 64-bit non-negative integers. Because the ASN.1 encoding of an integer always includes a sign bit, a signer can generate 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 TAMP messages before the space is exhausted, and it must then move to a different key pair. The ability to reset a sequence number with the Trust Anchor Update and Sequence Number Adjust messages is not there to avoid that transition; it is there to help recover from operational errors. When an apex or management trust anchor is replaced or removed, the storage for its sequence number SHOULD be reclaimed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request carries a counter. A store keeps the last counter it accepted from each sender and refuses anything lower, so an old request cannot be replayed. The counter is a 64-bit number, so it would take an enormous number of messages to run out.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The Trust Anchor Update Confirm, Apex Trust Anchor Update Confirm, Community Update Confirm, Sequence Number Adjust Confirm and TAMP Error messages carry a status code. There are many of them: success is 0, and the list runs through reasons such as a decoding failure, bad content, bad certificates, missing content, no trust anchor, not authorised, a bad digest or signature algorithm, an unsupported key size, a signature failure, insufficient memory, an unsupported TAMP message type, an improper trust anchor addition, a sequence number failure, a failure to decrypt the contingency public key, an incorrect target, a failure to find the trust anchor, an unsupported trust anchor algorithm or key size, a missing signature, busy resources, a version number mismatch, a missing policy set, a revoked certificate, an unsupported trust anchor format, an improper trust anchor change, a malformed message, a CMS error, an unsupported target identifier, and other at 127.

The success code says that an update, a part of an update, or an adjustment was processed successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: When an update does not work, the answer says why: the signature did not check out, the message was malformed, the signer was not allowed to manage that anchor, and so on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of this specification is about the syntax and meaning of TAMP messages. It relies on RFC 5914 for trust anchors, RFC 3852 for intermediate CMS content types and RFC 5280 for X.509 certificates. Because the TAMP messages that change the state of a trust anchor store are always signed by a trust anchor manager, no further integrity or origin authentication mechanism is needed, and the same is true of certificates. Trust anchor configurations and the certificates of managers and stores are not intended to be sensitive, so the specification provides no confidentiality for TAMP messages.

Security factors outside the scope of the specification greatly affect the assurance provided. The procedures a certification authority uses to validate the binding of an identity to its public key matter a great deal, particularly when it issues certificates to other authorities. In TAMP, issuing an end entity certificate under a management trust anchor is an act of delegation, but such an end entity cannot delegate further. Issuing a certificate for an authority under a management trust anchor is a delegation that can be delegated again, and the scope of it can be limited by certificate extensions.

Certification path construction compares distinguished names, and inconsistent use of name comparison rules can lead to invalid paths being accepted or valid ones rejected. To keep that complexity out of trust anchor stores, any certificate profile used with TAMP SHOULD use simple name structures and impose strict rules on acceptable distinguished names, including how they are encoded, with the aim of enabling simple binary comparison: case conversion, character set conversion, white space compression and trimming of leading and trailing white space SHOULD be avoided.

Some signature algorithms, such as DSA, need random one-time values, and generating key pairs needs random numbers. An inadequate random number generator can leave little or no security, because an attacker may find it easier to reproduce the random number generation environment and search the resulting small set of possibilities than to search the whole space.

The compromise of each kind of private key has its own effect. Compromising an identity trust anchor private key lets an unauthorised party issue certificates that every store configured with that anchor will accept, limited only by the certification path controls on the anchor. Compromising a management trust anchor private key lets an unauthorised party generate signed messages that every store with that anchor will accept, and every device holding it can be configured as the attacker wishes within the limits of the subordination checks. Compromising the apex trust anchor operational private key has the same effect for the stores that hold that apex anchor, and the attacker can then generate signed messages of any content type. The optional contingency private key offers a way to recover from that last case.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol signs everything that matters, so a stolen key is the main risk. Losing the management key lets an attacker reprogram every device that trusts it, and losing the apex key is worse. The RFC also says that the randomness and the naming rules of the certificates behind the anchors matter as much as the protocol itself.

messages.label: TAMP Status Query
messages.note: Asks which trust anchors are installed and which communities the store belongs to.

messages.label: TAMP Status Response
messages.note: A terse or a verbose answer, depending on what the query asked for.

messages.label: Trust Anchor Update
messages.note: Adds, modifies or removes trust anchors.

messages.label: Trust Anchor Update Confirm

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF TRUST ANCHOR

items.title: Apex
items.text: The ultimate authority over one trust anchor store. Its key may be replaced with a special message, and it may carry a contingency key for that purpose.

items.title: Management
items.text: Used to manage cryptographic modules. TAMP messages and signed firmware packages are validated to a management trust anchor.

items.title: Identity
items.text: The trust anchor of a public key infrastructure. It validates certification paths and is mostly used for certificates outside management.

children.label: Cryptographic module
children.note: Holds the private key that signs responses.

children.label: Trust anchor store
children.note: Holds the trust anchors, the communities and the sequence numbers.

children.label: TAMP processing
children.note: Runs the protocol: finds anchors, checks signatures, updates the store.

children.label: Application-specific processing
children.note: The rest of the device, which uses the trust anchors for its own work.

viz.caption: SUMMARY OF THE CMS WRAPPER FOR A SIGNED TAMP MESSAGE

data.title: CMS encapsulation

items.title: Only goes up
items.text: Each originator treats its sequence number as a number that never decreases.

items.title: Must be higher
items.text: A store rejects a message whose number is not greater than the last one it accepted from that sender.

items.title: One exception
items.text: The Sequence Number Adjust message is valid with the same number as the last one.

items.title: 64-bit
items.text: The number is a 64-bit non-negative integer, so it takes an enormous number of messages to run out.

items.title: Reset for recovery
items.text: An update or an adjust can reset the number, to recover from operational mistakes.

viz.caption: SOME OF THE TAMP STATUS CODES

items.label: success
items.desc: The update, part of an update, or the adjustment was processed successfully.

items.label: noTrustAnchor
items.desc: No suitable trust anchor was found.

items.label: notAuthorized
items.desc: The signer is not allowed to manage that trust anchor.

items.label: signatureFailure
items.desc: The digital signature did not validate.

items.label: seqNumFailure
items.desc: The sequence number was not higher than the last one accepted.

items.label: incorrectTarget
items.desc: The store is not an intended recipient of the message.

items.label: other
items.desc: The failure does not fit any other code.
